newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russian parliament resumes, Yeltsin faces attacks.
newsitem.headline: Russian parliament resumes, Yeltsin faces attacks.

text.p: Russian parliamentarians get back to work on Wednesday with the Communist-led State Duma expected to be a forum for attacks on hospital-bound President Boris Yeltsin and his government.

Gennady Seleznyov, Communist speaker of the Duma, the lower house, set the tone on Tuesday by repeating that he saw little chance of it approving Prime Minister Viktor Chernomyrdin's 1997 budget in its present form.
"The budget has not been thought through enough in a whole variety of important areas and so its chances of being accepted by the Duma are slim," he said.

This will be the first budget that the present parliament has been able to get its teeth into. The 1996 finance act was passed just before the successes of the Communists and their allies in last December's parliamentary elections.
It is also the first full parliamentary session since 65-year-old Yeltsin was reelected in July.

The strain of an arduous presidential election campaign to overcome what initially looked likely to be a Communist victory provoked a recurrence of Yeltsin's heart trouble which has kept the president out of sight since.

He is now likely to be more or less out of action for another four months, preparing for and then recovering from heart-bypass surgery. That will give his opponents in parliament plenty of scope for criticism.

Communist leader Gennady Zyuganov, who is due to give a news conference on Wednesday, has already called for Yeltsin to stand down. He said the July 3 vote was fraudulent because the Kremlin apparently concealed Yeltsin's new heart problems.
Chernomyrdin has maintained the relatively austere policies that have brought inflation under control and won a $10 billion credit from the International Monetary Fund.

But millions of workers, from miners to teachers, have not been paid for months and strikes are rumbling. So the government is under pressure to loosen purse strings and make good on some the promises that helped Yeltsin stay in office.

Chernomyrdin, 58, has already agreed to review defence spending after attacks from within the Kremlin itself in the shape of Yeltsin's security chief Alexander Lebed, who has warned that the army is on the verge of mutiny over pay.

After a new appeal for funds by Defence Minister Igor Rodionov, Yeltsin told the prime minister on Tuesday to convene a special cabinet meeting on army financing and announced that a new defence council would meet on Friday to discuss army reforms.
Lebed, 46, may be the star of the opening day of the Duma session. Legislators expect him to speak on the peace deal he reached on August 31 with Chechen separatist rebels.

The accord, which hinges on Lebed's agreement to withdraw Russian troops and leave the vexed question of the rebels' demand for independence open for five years, has met a less than fulsome welcome in Moscow. Both the government and its opponents say Lebed has not done enough to quash Chechen secessionism.
Separatist leader Zelimkhan Yandarbiyev is due in Moscow on Thursday or Friday for talks.
Lebed, an ex-general who wants to succeed Yeltsin, has often differed with government policy since his appointment in June.

On Tuesday, he sounded a tough line on NATO expansion before a trip to the alliance's headquarters next week and said Moscow should try to block the advance of the Islamic Taleban militia in Afghanistan.

Yeltsin has confirmed that Chernomyrdin, who will end a two-day visit to Switzerland on Wednesday, is to have formal control of the state, including the nuclear trigger, for a brief time while the president is undergoing his operation.
There is no sign of let-up, however, in the jostling for influence among Yeltsin's entourage, notably by Chernomyrdin and Lebed.
The Communists, described by Lebed this week as "decent people" with whome he could work, may see opportunity in that.
